system_prompt:
You are helping a Lead Product Manager triage an inbound request backlog for Trellis, a B2B ordering platform connecting food distributors with restaurant and hospitality operators.

Your job is to READ, not to score. You will tag every ticket and propose clusters. A human will review and edit every tag before any scoring happens, and the scoring itself is done by a separate deterministic formula. Do not output a priority score or a ranking. Confidence and account weight are inputs to the score, not the score.

Read all records together before tagging any of them. Several tickets may share a root cause that is only visible across records; look for that, but do not force clusters where the evidence is weak. Pay attention to date_received: note in reason when an item has been open for weeks without an owner, or when a ticket repeats an earlier complaint from the same account.

Definitions you must use:

classification
- "reactive": the item exists because an account reported a problem or asked for something.
- "proactive": self-originated by the product team, usually tied to a company metric.

cluster
- Group reactive tickets that most likely share ONE root cause and ONE fix. A cluster must have at least 2 tickets. Do not cluster by request_type alone; cluster by the mechanism that would be fixed. If two tickets look similar but are probably different bugs, keep them separate and say why in the evidence.
- Each cluster gets one shared effort_bucket (the cost of fixing the root cause once) and one confidence.
- Cluster confidence covers two doubts at once: how sure you are these tickets share one cause, and how well that cause is understood. Lower it for either.

severity (per ticket)
- Base this on the MEASURED or DESCRIBED effect in raw_notes, not the tone of the summary or the subject line, and not on who is copied on the email. "URGENT" in a subject line with "under 2% of orders affected" in the notes is low, not high.
- high: blocks orders or revenue for an account at scale, carries clear churn risk, or the account has escalated in a way that puts the relationship at risk.
- medium: real operational pain, workarounds exist, or affects a meaningful slice.
- low: cosmetic, rare, a workaround request, or a nice-to-have.
- For proactive items, severity means how urgent the metric problem is that the item addresses.

confidence (0.0 to 1.0)
- How well the root cause and fix are understood. Use exactly one of these four anchors so that runs are comparable; do not interpolate between them:
  0.9 = the notes confirm the cause and the fix is known (e.g. support reproduced it, a config value is named).
  0.7 = a specific cause is named and supported by evidence in the notes ("correlates with", "since the release", two tickets with matching signatures), but not confirmed.
  0.5 = a cause is guessed ("suspect", "possibly", "could be") or the notes offer two competing explanations.
  0.3 = cause unknown, hard to reproduce, or ownership is ambiguous (may not be our bug at all).
- For a cluster, the anchor covers both doubts: are these the same cause, and is the cause known. For proactive items: how confident you are it would move the named metric, on the same anchors.

effort_bucket
- One of: "small", "1-2 sprints", "large", "unclear". Take rough_effort_hint as the estimate: it comes from the team and is reliable by default. Map it to the nearest bucket and keep it.
- Override the hint only when something specific in the ticket contradicts it: the hint sizes a fix but the notes show the cause is unknown (then "unclear"), or the hint says "unclear" but the notes confirm the cause and the fix (then size it). A suspected or "could be" cause is not confirmation; keep "unclear" and say the investigation is urgent in reason. If you have no specific reason to override, keep the hint. Record every override in ambiguity_note with the reason.
- For a cluster, set effort from the members' hints: use the hint of the member whose notes best describe the cause and fix; if no member identifies a cause, use "unclear". Say which hint you used in the cluster evidence.

redirect (boolean)
- true when the item is not product/engineering work at all: a configuration change, a data cleanup, a process change with no engineering cost, or something support or infra should own. Explain in reason.

metric_linked (boolean)
- true only if the notes name a company metric the item moves.

retires (list of request_ids)
- For proactive items only: which reactive tickets in THIS backlog would this item structurally eliminate or prevent from recurring? Be strict. A self-service setup wizard does not fix a field-mapping bug. Detecting, monitoring, or surfacing a problem earlier does not count as eliminating it; leave such tickets out of retires and mention the detection-only link in ambiguity_note so the reviewer can decide. Leave empty for reactive items.

ambiguity_note
- Anything the human must decide: contradictions, missing facts, ownership questions, urgency claims that don't match the evidence, an effort hint you overrode, a detection-only link you left out of retires, or a claim of breadth ("other accounts have asked") with no supporting tickets in this backlog. Empty string if none.

cross_record_observations
- Patterns visible only by reading across tickets: the same bug reported as opposite symptoms, the same symptom at more than one account, stated urgency that contradicts measured impact, items that have sat unowned, and which proactive items map onto which reactive patterns. Be concrete and cite request_ids.

accounts
- You have no prior knowledge of these accounts. Derive each account's tier ONLY from what the summaries and raw_notes in this backlog say (phrases like "top-5 by GMV", "enterprise tier", "mid-market", "small regional, low GMV"). Return one entry per distinct source_account, copying source_account exactly as it appears in the data (same spelling, spacing and capitalisation, no abbreviation), with a tier of "top", "enterprise", "mid", "small", "internal", or "unknown", and quote the evidence. Use "unknown" when the notes give no tier signal; do not guess from the account name. Treat "Internal" (or any source that is the product team itself) as "internal".
- Also give a weight from 1 to 5 for the account's size. This is the revenue tier and nothing else: 5 for top or enterprise, 3 for mid-market, 1 for small, 3 for internal and for unknown. Do NOT adjust it for churn risk, escalations, growth, executive involvement or reputational exposure. Those belong to specific tickets and are captured by severity (a ticket tied to a churn-risk signal is high severity; a ticket that is not tied to it is not). Adjusting size for them would count the same fact twice. In weight_reason, state the tier and the phrase it came from.
- Separately, mark an account "strategic": true when the notes show it matters beyond its current revenue tier: fast growth that will outstrip the tier, a reference or lighthouse customer, a regulatory or partnership relationship, or a market the company is entering. This is account-level and forward-looking. Churn risk, escalations and executive involvement do NOT make an account strategic; they are per-ticket and belong in severity. Quote the phrase in strategic_reason; if there is no such signal, false with an empty reason.

Be specific and terse in every reason. Cite request_ids when you link tickets.

clusters.label: Punchout Integration Errors (Field Mapping / Session / Validation)
clusters.root_cause_hypothesis: Punchout connector configurations (ProcureFlow, VendorGate, CatalogBridge) have field-mapping or session-handling defects — possibly introduced or exposed by the last catalog release — causing checkout errors, blank carts, $0 pricing, and validation rejections across multiple accounts and connectors.
clusters.evidence: TRQ-1042: 'field-mapping mismatch introduced by our last release' (ProcureFlow, Meridian). TRQ-1050: blank cart on Safari/iPad (VendorGate, Cobalt). TRQ-1056: generic validation error above dollar threshold (ProcureFlow, Cobalt). TRQ-1061: $0.00 line-item pricing intermittently (CatalogBridge, Northwind). TRQ-1065: blank page on return URL post-checkout (ProcureFlow, Oakmere). All involve punchout checkout failures across different connectors and accounts. Effort hint used: 'unclear' from TRQ-1042 and TRQ-1056 (dominant — cause not confirmed across connectors); TRQ-1050/TRQ-1061 hint 'small' but those are symptoms, not confirmed causes. Reviewer note: TRQ-1061 uses CatalogBridge (different connector) and TRQ-1056 ownership is ambiguous — these may be separate bugs sharing a surface-level symptom.

clusters.label: ERP Timeout → Duplicate Order Submission
clusters.root_cause_hypothesis: When the ERP integration times out (during batch windows or intermittently), retry logic fires and submits the order a second time, creating duplicate orders and requiring manual credit memos.
clusters.evidence: TRQ-1043: 'retry logic firing when Northwind's ERP times out during morning batch window' — third recurrence this quarter. TRQ-1054: 'SAP integration timing out intermittently, causing orders to be submitted twice about once a week' (Meridian). Both describe timeout → duplicate submission mechanism. Effort hint used: '1-2 sprints' from TRQ-1043 (cause best described there); TRQ-1054 matches. Reviewer should confirm if Northwind and Meridian use the same integration code path.

clusters.label: ERP Feed Rate-Limiting by Trellis Config
clusters.root_cause_hypothesis: Trellis-side rate-limit configuration is throttling legitimate ERP order batches — either because the config threshold is too low for month-end volume (TRQ-1049) or because a new ERP's IP range was never added to the allowlist (TRQ-1062).
clusters.evidence: TRQ-1049: 'our own rate-limit config, not their retry behavior' — SFTP feed throttled at month-end (Northwind). TRQ-1062: 'new ERP's IP range not on allowlist' — legitimate batches throttled post-migration (Cobalt). Both are Trellis-side config issues causing order throttling, not ERP-side bugs. Effort hint used: 'small' from both tickets (config changes). TRQ-1062 is a redirect (config-only); TRQ-1049 may require a config change plus review of rate-limit logic.

clusters.label: Lead-Time Consolidation Logic Bug (Multi-Supplier Standing Orders)
clusters.root_cause_hypothesis: The lead-time consolidation logic for multi-supplier standing orders does not correctly select the longest lead-time item, causing orders to be scheduled either a day late (TRQ-1046, picks wrong item) or using the shortest lead time (TRQ-1060, inverse manifestation) — both pointing to the same faulty selection logic.
clusters.evidence: TRQ-1046: 'lead-time consolidation logic isn't picking the longest lead-time item correctly when an order spans multiple suppliers' (Palisade). TRQ-1060: 'scheduled using the shortest lead time across suppliers instead of the longest' (Meridian) — notes explicitly say 'inverse of the Palisade lead-time bug (TRQ-1046), worth checking if same underlying logic bug.' Effort hint used: '1-2 sprints' from TRQ-1046 (cause best described there); TRQ-1060 matches.

clusters.label: Inventory Status Sync Inaccuracy (In-Stock / Out-of-Stock Mismatch)
clusters.root_cause_hypothesis: Inventory availability shown to buyers is not reliably reflecting actual stock levels — buyers see items as available that are actually out-of-stock or backordered, suggesting a platform-side sync latency or feed-processing bug affecting multiple accounts.
clusters.evidence: TRQ-1047: 'inventory status shown to buyers doesn't match what's actually available — buyers ordering out-of-stock items and getting cancellation notices' (Oakmere); notes flag 'broader sync-flakiness pattern worth checking.' TRQ-1058: 'in stock items actually backordered, leading to last-minute substitutions for banquet events' (Palisade). Same symptom (stale inventory display) at two different account tiers. Effort hint used: '1-2 sprints' from TRQ-1058 (larger account, more detail); TRQ-1047 hint is 'unclear' — cause not confirmed, so cluster confidence is held at 0.5.

clusters.label: Catalog / Tag-Mapping Disputes (SKU Mis-mapping Across Accounts)
clusters.root_cause_hypothesis: SKU tag mappings between supplier catalog tags and internal commodity codes are systematically incorrect or unmaintained, causing wrong reorder suggestions, promotional filter exclusions, unit-of-measure conflicts, and post-migration mis-maps — affecting nearly every account this quarter.
clusters.evidence: TRQ-1044: 40+ SKUs mis-mapped between commodity codes and supplier tags (Cobalt). TRQ-1052: seasonal produce under wrong commodity tags, excluded from promotional filter — second complaint from Palisade in 60 days; possibly systemic across seasonal SKUs. TRQ-1059: conflicting units of measure (case vs. each) for same item code across two supplier catalogs (Oakmere). TRQ-1066: ~200 SKUs mis-mapped post supplier catalog migration (Meridian). Pattern spans four accounts and multiple request types. Effort hint used: 'unclear' from TRQ-1052 (systemic scope unknown); TRQ-1044 hint 'small' and TRQ-1066 '1-2 sprints' apply to individual fixes but systemic scope is unclear.

clusters.label: Standing Order Scheduler Silent Failures (No Alerting)
clusters.root_cause_hypothesis: The standing order scheduler silently fails without alerting — causing orders to either not fire at all (TRQ-1053) or skip a week and double up the next (TRQ-1068) — with no visibility to account managers or buyers until the impact is noticed manually.
clusters.evidence: TRQ-1053: 'scheduler task silently failed with no alerting' — standing order didn't fire (Oakmere); support confirmed cause; notes flag monitoring gap. TRQ-1068: 'standing orders occasionally skip a scheduled week entirely with no failure notification, then double up the following week' (Northwind) — notes say 'similar signature to TRQ-1053, possibly same root cause.' Effort hint used: 'small' from TRQ-1053 (cause confirmed there); TRQ-1068 hint is 'unclear' — if same root cause, small fix applies; if different trigger at scale, effort may be larger. Confidence 0.5 because TRQ-1068 cause is not confirmed.

cross_record_observations: SAME BUG, OPPOSITE SYMPTOMS (lead-time logic): TRQ-1046 (Palisade) reports standing orders scheduled a day LATE; TRQ-1060 (Meridian) reports orders scheduled using the SHORTEST lead time instead of longest. Notes on TRQ-1060 explicitly flag this as the inverse of TRQ-1046. Both point to the same lead-time consolidation logic selecting the wrong item — one fix should cover both.

SAME SYMPTOM, MULTIPLE ACCOUNTS (inventory sync): TRQ-1047 (Oakmere, small) and TRQ-1058 (Palisade, enterprise) both report buyers seeing incorrect in-stock status leading to cancellations or last-minute substitutions. TRQ-1047 notes flag 'broader sync-flakiness pattern worth checking against other accounts' — TRQ-1058 confirms the pattern is not isolated to a small account.

SAME SYMPTOM, MULTIPLE ACCOUNTS (scheduler silent failure): TRQ-1053 (Oakmere) and TRQ-1068 (Northwind) both describe standing orders silently failing with no alerting. TRQ-1068 notes explicitly reference TRQ-1053 as a matching signature. The monitoring gap flagged in TRQ-1053 is now confirmed as a cross-account risk by TRQ-1068.

STATED URGENCY CONTRADICTS MEASURED IMPACT: TRQ-1050 (Cobalt, 'URGENT — buyers can't order') affects under 2% of orders per analytics. TRQ-1061 (Northwind, reported as urgent) affects only a handful of transactions per week per logs. Both should be triaged at low severity despite urgent framing.

CATALOG TAG-MAPPING IS A CROSS-ACCOUNT PATTERN: TRQ-1044 (Cobalt), TRQ-1052 (Palisade), TRQ-1059 (Oakmere), and TRQ-1066 (Meridian) all report SKU mis-mapping issues within a single quarter. The proactive initiative TRQ-1063 directly targets this pattern. TRQ-1052 notes flag possible systemic scope across seasonal SKUs beyond any single account.

NORTHWIND HAS THREE DISTINCT ISSUES OPEN SIMULTANEOUSLY: TRQ-1043 (duplicate orders from retry logic), TRQ-1049 (rate-limit throttling), and TRQ-1055 (bulk-edit feature request) — plus TRQ-1061 (punchout pricing) and TRQ-1068 (scheduler skip). High complaint volume relative to mid-market size (noted in TRQ-1043) is borne out by the backlog volume. Reviewer should assess relationship health.

TRQ-1054 (Meridian SAP duplicate orders) was informally open for weeks before formal logging on Jun 30 — a top-5 GMV account's issue festering without an owner is a relationship risk. Similarly, TRQ-1062 (Cobalt allowlist config) has sat unowned for three weeks as of its date; it is a redirect but needs immediate assignment.

PROACTIVE INITIATIVES MAP ONTO REACTIVE CLUSTERS: TRQ-1045 (self-service punchout wizard) targets the punchout_field_mapping cluster (TRQ-1042, TRQ-1050, TRQ-1056, TRQ-1061, TRQ-1065). TRQ-1063 (self-serve tag-mapping tool) targets the catalog_tag_mapping cluster (TRQ-1044, TRQ-1052, TRQ-1059, TRQ-1066). TRQ-1057 (standing-order health score) is detection-only for the scheduler_silent_failure and lead_time_logic clusters — it would surface failures earlier but not fix the underlying bugs.

PUNCHOUT ISSUES SPAN THREE DIFFERENT CONNECTORS: TRQ-1042/TRQ-1056/TRQ-1065 involve ProcureFlow; TRQ-1050 involves VendorGate; TRQ-1061 involves CatalogBridge. While clustered together as punchout_field_mapping, the multi-connector spread reduces confidence that a single fix covers all — reviewer should assess whether connector-specific bugs are being conflated.
